cards.explanation: The answer is that he would die. The LORD tells Moses, Israel's leader, that Aaron, Israel's high priest, must not enter freely, “…or else he will die…” (Leviticus 16:2). That is plain and serious. Notice the word “freely,” too, friends. The rest of the chapter spells out exactly how Aaron does go in.

The answer is False. Leviticus 16:4 says, “…he must bathe himself with water before he wears them.” The garments are holy, so Aaron washes first. Order matters in this chapter, friends, and this is the very first step you can see him taking.

The answer is himself and his household. The text says Aaron is to present the bull “…and make atonement for himself and his household.” (Leviticus 16:6). So the first sin offering covers Aaron and his own house. The people's sin offering comes later, with a goat (Leviticus 16:15).

The answer is that it is sent into the wilderness. The scapegoat is presented alive before the LORD “…to make atonement by sending it into the wilderness as the scapegoat.” (Leviticus 16:10). One goat is sacrificed and the other is sent away alive. Two goats, two different jobs, friends.

The answer is mercy seat. Verse 13 says the cloud of incense “…will cover the mercy seat above the Testimony…” This is the same mercy seat from verse 2, where the LORD says He appears in the cloud. Aaron brings the incense to the place the LORD named.

The answer is True. Leviticus 16:13 says the cloud of incense will cover the mercy seat, “…so that he will not die.” That ties right back to the warning in verse 2, friends. Aaron brings the incense in with him, and the cloud is there for his sake.

The answer is that he sprinkles it like the bull's blood. The text says Aaron “…must do as he did with the bull’s blood: He is to sprinkle it against the mercy seat and in front of it.” (Leviticus 16:15). Same move, different animal. The bull was for his own sin offering and this goat is for the people's.

The answer is the sins of the Israelites. The LORD says Aaron makes atonement for the Most Holy Place “…because of the impurities and rebellious acts of the Israelites in regard to all their sins.” (Leviticus 16:16). The text names the Israelites and says all their sins. Even the holy place is part of this, friends.

The answer is False. Verse 17 says, “No one may be in the Tent of Meeting from the time Aaron goes in to make atonement in the Most Holy Place until he leaves…” That covers the whole time he is making atonement for himself, his household and the whole assembly of Israel. Aaron goes in, and the Tent of Meeting stays empty of everyone else.

The answer is to cleanse it from Israel's uncleanness. Aaron sprinkles the blood on it seven times “…to cleanse it and consecrate it from the uncleanness of the Israelites.” (Leviticus 16:19). The altar gets cleansed and consecrated. Earlier, Aaron also makes atonement for the Most Holy Place and the Tent of Meeting (Leviticus 16:16), and the altar is part of that same day's work.

The answer is that he confesses all Israel's sins over it. Aaron lays both hands on the live goat's head and confesses over it “…all the iniquities and rebellious acts of the Israelites in regard to all their sins.” (Leviticus 16:21). Then a man appointed for the task sends the goat away, and it carries those sins into a solitary place (Leviticus 16:22). I think those hands stay on that goat a while, friends, because that's a lot of confessing.

The answer is his burnt offering and the people's. Once he's in his own clothes, Aaron goes out and sacrifices “…his burnt offering and the people’s burnt offering to make atonement for himself and for the people.” (Leviticus 16:24). The people have their burnt offering too. Both are done in his regular clothes, after the bath.

The answer is to wash his clothes and bathe. The man who released the goat “…must wash his clothes and bathe himself with water; afterward he may reenter the camp.” (Leviticus 16:26). Clothes first, bath too, and only THEN back into the camp. The text doesn't say why, so I'll just say it's a very thorough cleanup, friends. I've gotten dough all over this mustache and I still only got a rag.

The answer is that everything left is burned up. The bull and the goat, whose blood was brought into the Most Holy Place, are taken outside the camp, “and their hides, flesh, and dung must be burned up.” (Leviticus 16:27). Hides, flesh and dung, all three named for the fire. When my oven burns a batch, I at least get a few sad crumbs. This fire is much more thorough than mine.

The answer is humble. The LORD says, “…you shall humble yourselves and not do any work…” (Leviticus 16:29). Verse 31 repeats it: “…that you may humble yourselves…” The day is set apart, friends, and humbling comes with it.

The answer is False. Leviticus 16:29 says that on the tenth day of the seventh month, no work gets done, “…whether the native or the foreigner who resides among you…” The foreigner living among them is included in the rule. Everybody takes the day.

The answer is that atonement will be made to cleanse them. The LORD says, “…on this day atonement will be made for you to cleanse you, and you will be clean from all your sins before the LORD.” (Leviticus 16:30). That is the reason given, friends. The whole day is about atonement and being made clean.

The answer is the priest ordained to succeed his father. Verse 32 says, “The priest who is anointed and ordained to succeed his father as high priest shall make atonement.” So this isn't a one time job for Aaron. It gets passed on, and the next high priest puts on the sacred linen garments too.

The answer is once. The LORD says it is “…to make atonement once a year for the Israelites because of all their sins.” (Leviticus 16:34). One day a year, friends, and it's a permanent statute. That's why the tenth day of the seventh month matters so much.
